growth_story.headline: Kosovo's income per person has grown 5.1 percent a year since 2009, carried by diaspora money, household spending and credit, and is at its highest yet.
growth_story.arc: Since 2009, Kosovo's income per person has grown 5.1 percent a year on average with no lasting break, and in 2025 it reached its highest level yet, more than double its 2008 level. Growth averaged 4.8 percent a year over 2009 to 2015 and 5.4 percent over 2016 to 2025. It dipped to 0.9 percent in 2012, fell 5.4 percent in 2020 and rebounded 11.0 percent in 2021. The World Bank describes a shift away from aid toward growth driven by consumption, infrastructure investment and fast-growing credit, and domestic credit to the private sector rose from 37.3 percent of GDP in 2015 to 65.6 percent in 2025. Money from Kosovars abroad sits under much of this: remittances support household spending, and most foreign investment goes into real estate paid for by the diaspora. Growth in income per person slowed to 4.7 percent in 2025, a year of political stalemate after the February elections, and rising prices weighed on activity in 2026.

threads.title: Diaspora money behind spending
threads.text: Money sent home by Kosovars abroad reaches many households. The IMF says the gap in the current account has been paid for by borrowing and by investment from the diaspora in sectors that do not trade abroad, most of it in real estate.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe steady, moderate growth in total output in recent years and a modest slowing in 2025. The data show income per person growing much faster, by 9.4 percent in 2023 and 10.4 percent in 2024. Income per person can only grow faster than total output if the number of people counted fell. The sources read here do not discuss population change, so they do not explain this gap.
